challenges.name: package-that-didnt-exist-evidence
challenges.title: The Package That Didn't Exist: read the evidence
challenges.description: An AI assistant suggested @codedev-ui/form-utils in a pull request; CodeDev owns @codedev, not @codedev-ui. The dependency checker passed it, and three days later a stranger registered the scope and published a version with a postinstall script that read the build's environment. Six statements on one evidence pack - the PR diff (A), the CI log (B), the registry history (C), the checker code (D) and the lockfile (E) - take you from reading the evidence to a hypothesis, past two wrong explanations, to the fix and its verification.

questions.explanation: True. In both runs the only check-deps line that names the package is "owned scope, skipped", and in D that log call is followed by continue, before checked++ and before published.has(name). So the package was never compared with the registry snapshot: on Monday, when it did not exist, the checker could not have reported it as not found. The misconception is to read PASS as "every dependency was checked and is fine"; PASS only means none of the checked ones failed.

False. 36 + 2 = 38, not 41: three entries were neither checked nor logged. They are scoped packages outside @codedev, such as @tanstack/react-query in A: they do not start with @codedev, and NAME has no room for "@scope/", so the second continue drops them without a word. A checker that skips silently is worse than one that fails, because its PASS looks the same either way. The habit to build: check that the counts in a CI summary add up, and make a checker report every input it saw.

True. startsWith compares characters, not scopes: "@codedev-ui", "@codedevs" and "@codedev.ui" all start with "@codedev". The scope of a scoped name is the text up to the first "/", and it must be compared as a whole string with the owned list. This is the root cause; the regex that silently drops other scoped names is the second bug in the same loop. The common mistake is to treat a prefix as ownership: on a public registry anyone can register any scope name nobody has taken yet, including one that looks like yours.

questions.question:
Evidence C - registry history, npm view @codedev-ui/form-utils time --json:
{
  "created": "2026-10-15T08:14:03.512Z",
  "1.2.0":   "2026-10-15T08:14:03.512Z",
  "1.2.1":   "2026-10-15T08:41:27.904Z"
}
npm view @codedev-ui/form-utils@1.2.0 scripts   -> (none)
npm view @codedev-ui/form-utils@1.2.1 scripts   -> { postinstall: 'node ./scripts/setup.js' }

Evidence B - CI job "install" on PR #1184:
run 1  Mon 2026-10-12 10:52 UTC
  [check-deps] owned scope, skipped: @codedev/ui-kit
  [check-deps] owned scope, skipped: @codedev-ui/form-utils
  [check-deps] 41 dependencies, 36 checked, 0 not found: PASS
  [npm ci] npm error Missing: @codedev-ui/form-utils@^1.2.0 from lock file
run 2  Thu 2026-10-15 09:38 UTC (after "update lockfile" at 09:31)
  [check-deps] owned scope, skipped: @codedev/ui-kit
  [check-deps] owned scope, skipped: @codedev-ui/form-utils
  [check-deps] 41 dependencies, 36 checked, 0 not found: PASS
  [npm ci] npm info run @codedev-ui/form-utils@1.2.1 postinstall node_modules/@codedev-ui/form-utils node ./scripts/setup.js
  [egress] 09:39:02 CONNECT collect.formutils-cdn.example:443 from runner ci-07

Statement: "Running npm audit in the CI job would have stopped the Thursday install, because the package ran a postinstall script that read environment variables."
questions.explanation: False. npm audit compares the installed versions with published security advisories. Version 1.2.1 had existed for under an hour when run 2 installed it (08:41 to 09:38), no advisory named it, and audit does not read install scripts or watch what they do. A new malicious package is exactly the case audit cannot see. The checks that would have caught it are about names and provenance: an unknown scope, a package created after the PR was opened, and an install script on a dependency nobody reviewed.

False. The lockfile was generated by npm install on Thursday at 09:31, 50 minutes after 1.2.1 was published, so it recorded whatever the registry served then: the attacker's version. An integrity hash proves that later installs get the same bytes, not that the bytes are trustworthy; nobody reviewed them. The lockfile even carried a warning sign, "hasInstallScript": true, on a brand-new dependency. Lockfiles protect against drift, not against a bad first resolution.

Statement: "A regression test for the fix should run the checker on the PR's dependencies with a registry snapshot that contains @codedev-ui/form-utils, and expect it to be reported as an unknown scope."
questions.explanation: True. On Thursday the package existed, so a test that only expects "not found" would pass on Monday's snapshot and miss the attack three days later. Reporting the scope itself as unknown blocks the name whether or not someone has registered it yet. The same test should also expect a finding for every one of the 41 entries, so a silent skip can never come back. The misconception is to test the fix only against the evidence of the first day.

challenges.name: scoped-name-checker
challenges.title: Fix the dependency checker that skipped scoped names
challenges.description: An AI assistant added "@codedev-ui/form-utils" to CodeDev's package.json. CodeDev owns the npm scope @codedev, not @codedev-ui. The CI step check-deps logged "owned scope, skipped: @codedev-ui/form-utils" and "41 dependencies, 36 checked, 0 not found: PASS"; three days later a stranger registered @codedev-ui and published a version whose postinstall script read the build's environment variables. Fix checkDependencies(dependencies, policy, registry) so that it returns exactly one finding per entry of dependencies, in input order: { dependency, package, status }. dependency is the key in package.json. package is the package npm installs: the key itself, or for an alias ("key": "npm:<name>@<range>", or "npm:<name>" without a range) the <name> after "npm:" - a scoped name starts with "@", so the "@" before the range is the first "@" after the first character; package is "" when the status is invalid. status is the first rule that applies: "invalid" when the key or the package is not a valid name (valid: "<part>" or "@<part>/<part>", where <part> starts with a-z or 0-9 and continues with a-z 0-9 . _ -, at most 214 characters in total); "unknown_scope" when the package is scoped and its scope (the text before the first "/", e.g. "@codedev") is not one of policy.ownedScopes or policy.knownScopes, compared as whole strings; "not_found" when the package is not in the registry snapshot (a list of names; scoped packages of owned or known scopes are looked up too); otherwise "ok". The range part of a spec is not checked. The runner reads { ownedScopes, knownScopes, registry, dependencies } and prints the findings as JSON.
hints: How many findings come back for a package.json with 8 dependencies, and which entries never reach the registry lookup? What does it take for a scope to be yours, rather than to start with the same letters as yours?

Look at the two `continue` lines at the top of the loop: one compares scopes with startsWith, the other tests the key with a pattern that has no room for "@scope/". Then look at `spec`: is it ever read? An alias installs the package named after "npm:", not the key.

A similar case with other names: owned ["@acme"], known ["@types"]. "@acme/core" has the scope "@acme" (the text before the first "/"): owned. "@acme-tools/core" has the scope "@acme-tools", which is not equal to "@acme", so it is an unknown scope although it starts with "@acme". "web": "npm:@acme/web-legacy@2.0.0" installs "@acme/web-legacy": searching for "@" from the second character finds the one before 2.0.0. "pad": "npm:left-pad" installs "left-pad". Each of them still gets one finding.

tests.name: The incident PR: a scope that only looks like CodeDev's is reported, every entry gets a finding
Unscoped and @types packages: a hallucinated name is not found, the rest are ok
Lookalike scopes are unknown even after someone published them; two owned scopes are fine
npm: aliases are checked by the package they install, scoped or not, with or without a range
Owned and known scopes are still looked up: a missing @codedev package is not found
Invalid names and aliases: uppercase, empty scope or name, leading dot or underscore, 215 chars
Large manifest: about 590 dependencies in every name form
